en: Now, the *Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā*: this work is by the master Vasubandhu.
For the various metaphorical designations of self and phenomena that proceed...
This transformation occurs within the transformation of consciousness, and that transformation is threefold.
There is the maturation, that which is called mentation, and the representation of objects.
Among these, the consciousness called the storehouse (ālaya) is the maturation and contains all seeds.
And that [storehouse consciousness] has perceptions of appropriation and location that are not consciously perceived;
it is always accompanied by contact, mental attention, feeling, perception, and volition.
Therein the feeling is equanimity, and that [mind] is unobscured-neutral;
likewise for contact and the other [mental factors], and it proceeds like the current of a stream.
Its cessation occurs in arhatship;
based upon that [cessation], there proceeds the consciousness called "mind" (manas), which has that as its object and consists of mentation.
It is always accompanied by four afflictions that are obscured and indeterminate,
known as self-view, self-delusion, self-pride, and self-love.
That [mental consciousness] does not exist for an Arhat in those [realms] where it is born, nor with other [objects] such as touch that consist of those [realms];
nor does it exist during the attainment of cessation, nor on the supramundane path.
This is the second transformation; the third is that perception of the sixfold object which is wholesome, unwholesome, or neither.
It is associated with the universal mental factors, the specific ones, and the wholesome ones;
likewise, it is associated with the afflictions and the secondary afflictions, and it possesses the three types of feeling.

The first [mental factors] are contact and so forth; then desire, resolve, mindfulness, along with concentration and wisdom, which are the determinate [factors]; and furthermore, faith, shame, and dread of blame. (Tvk 10)
The three beginning with non-attachment, vigor, pliancy accompanied by vigilance, and non-harming are the wholesome [factors]. The afflictions are attachment, aversion, and delusion. (Tvk 11)
Pride, views, and doubt; furthermore, anger and enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, along with deceit; Tvk 12.
Deceit, arrogance, lack of non-violence, lack of shame, lack of dread,
lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, then laziness, negligence, and lost mindfulness.
Distraction, lack of clear comprehension, remorse, torpor, applied thought,
and sustained thought— these secondary afflictions are twofold within the two [categories].
The arising of the five consciousnesses within the root-consciousness occurs according to conditions, either simultaneously or not, just as waves arise upon the water.
The arising of mental consciousness occurs at all times, except for those in the state of non-perception (asañjñika),
the two meditative attainments (samāpatti), torpor (middha), and unconsciousness due to fainting (mūrchana).
This transformation of consciousness is conceptual construction; that which is conceptually constructed by it does not exist. Therefore, all this is representation-only.
For consciousness contains all seeds; its transformation proceeds in such and such a way through mutual influence, whereby this or that conceptual construction arises.
The latent impressions of karma, together with the impressions of the twofold grasping,
produce another maturation once the previous maturation has been exhausted.
Whatever object is conceptualized by whichever conceptualization, that is merely the imagined nature; it does not exist.
The dependent nature, however, is conceptual construction arising from conditions;
the perfected nature is its constant absence of the former.
For this very reason, it is neither different nor non-different from the dependent nature;
it is to be described like impermanence and so forth, for as long as this [perfected nature] is not perceived, that [dependent nature] is not seen.
Having in mind the threefold absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) of the threefold intrinsic nature,
the absence of intrinsic nature of all phenomena was taught.

The first is without intrinsic nature by its very definition; furthermore, the other is the absence of intrinsic nature because it does not exist by itself. This is another form of the lack of intrinsic nature.
That which is the ultimate reality of all phenomena is also suchness (tathatā), because it remains as it is at all times; that very state is itself representation-only (vijñaptimātratā).
As long as consciousness does not abide in the state of representation-only,
the latent tendency toward the twofold grasping will not cease.
Even when one maintains that "this is representation-only" based on perception,
if one places something before oneself, one does not abide in that state of representation-only.
When consciousness no longer perceives any objective support,
then it abides in the state of mere-consciousness (vijñaptimātra), because in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping.
This is mindless and without apprehension; it is supramundane gnosis.
It is the revolution of the basis through the twofold abandonment of corruption.
That very same outflow-free realm is inconceivable, wholesome, and eternal;
it is blissful, the body of liberation, and this is called the Dharma-body of the Great Sage.
The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā is completed. This is the work of the Master Vasubandhu.
